text:
The old miller, Elias, had hands like cracked earth and pockets full of nothing but dust. Yet, every autumn, he shared his last sacks of flour with the village baker, who was always short on grain before winter’s bite. “Why?” the neighbors asked, eyes narrowing at Elias’s empty larder. “You give away what you barely have.”

Elias smiled, a fragile thing like dry leaf. “I do not give to be remembered,” he said. “I give because I remember.”

He spoke of his own childhood, when hunger was a wolf in the house, and how a stranger’s bread had been the only light in that dark den. That kindness had etched itself into his soul, a scar that healed into wisdom. He passed the flour not as charity, but as tribute.

Years later, when Elias lay dying, the baker arrived with warm loaves, breaking them over the miller’s chest. The scent filled the room, carrying Elias back to that long-ago kitchen, back to the moment he first learned that survival is not solitary. Generosity, he realized then, is not forgetting one’s need; it is remembering another’s grace so vividly that your own hands become instruments of its echo.
